"'''Groovin{{'-}}'''" is a song written by American singer-songwriters [[Felix Cavaliere]] and [[Eddie Brigati]], initially recorded by their group [[the Young Rascals]] in 1967. Cavaliere was inspired to compose the song by his girlfriend Adrienne Buccheri, whom he only got to meet on Sundays amidst heavy touring and recording. Musically, the song differs from most of the band's previous output, leaving the [[garage rock]] genre for [[Latin American]] influences, such as [[Baião (music)|baião]]. Lyrically, "Groovin{{'"}} tells the tale of a narrator spending time with his partner on a Sunday afternoon. The song was arranged and recorded at the Talentmasters Studios, [[New York City]] in March of 1967.

Initially, [[Atlantic Records]] were skeptical of releasing "Groovin{{'"}} as a single, given that it deviated from their previous output. After hearing it, the disc jockey [[Murray the K]] convinced [[Jerry Wexler]] to release it. "Groovin{{'"}} was released as a single on April 10, 1967, [[A-side and B-side|backed by]] "Sueño". It became a commercial hit, reaching number-one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in May 1967. It peaked at number eight in the UK as the Young Rascals' only hit there.

Upon initial release, "Groovin{{'"}} received widespread critical acclaim by critics, who noted the new direction the Young Rascals took with the single. Owing to the success, it became the [[Groovin' (The Young Rascals album)|title track of the band's third studio album]]. Retrospective appraisal of the single have often noted the experimental nature of the single. Shortly after the release of the original, [[Booker T. & the M.G.'s]] recorded a cover that reached number 21 on [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], while [[War (American band)|War]] and [[Pato Banton]] have seen success with their versions. The Young Rascals original version is on the [[the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll|500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll]] list and has been awarded a [[List of Grammy Hall of Fame Award recipients E-I|Grammy Hall of Fame Award]].

sections.heading: Background and writing
Composition
sections.wikitext:
Lyrically, "Groovin{{'"}} is the evocation of a person in love through the laid-back perspective of someone who would do nothing but spend time with his romantic partner during a Sunday afternoon.{{Sfn|Myers|2013}}''<ref name="pc52">{{Gilliland|url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc19834/m1/|title=Show 52 - The Soul Reformation: Phase three, soul music at the summit. [Part 8]|show=52|track=5}}</ref>'' The laid-back narrative is conveyed even though the narrator suggests to his partner that he'd like to walk through crowded avenues and meet strangers that are happy.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=152}} However, the narrator laments the fact the Sunday afternoon will end, in dismay over the fact that it passed by so quickly.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=152}} The phrase "you and me endlessly" which appears in the final verse was often misheard as the [[mondegreen]] "you and me and Leslie", which according to Caveliere was a result of his habit of slurring "uneven words to squeeze them in to fit the beats", something that was hampered by the fact that a conga fill appeared just as the word "endlessly" was sung.{{Sfn|Myers|2013}}

Musically, as performed by the Young Rascals, "Groovin{{'"}} is performed in [[F minor]], and has a BPM of 108.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} The song sports a clear structure, with the chorus repeated three times, supported by three verses.{{Sfn|Myers|2013}} Structurally, it is largely composed of the chords of [[D (musical note)|D]] and [[E♭ (musical note)|E♭]] that are performed by Cavaliere on his piano during the choruses in a [[Time signature|{{music|time|6|8}} time signature]] before alternating.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} During the verses, the chord of [[F♯ (musical note)|F♯]] largely substitutes the chord of D, though also marks the appearance of the chords of [[G (musical note)|G]] and [[A (musical note)|A]] through a [[Modulation (music)|modulation]] that appears towards the end of the verses.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} "Groovin{{'"}} bears a strong inspiration from [[Afro-Cuban music]],{{Sfn|Rhino|2021}} particularly concerning its [[Baião (music)|baião]] rhythm and instrumentation which was unconventional for the band.{{Sfn|Myers|2016|p=88}} It features the use of conga drums played by drummer [[Dino Danelli]] and tambourine by Cornish rather than a more standard drum set.{{Sfn|Myers|2016|p=88}}

Musically, as performed by the Young Rascals, "Groovin{{'"}} is performed in F minor, and has a BPM of 108.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} The song sports a clear structure, with the chorus repeated three times, supported by three verses.{{Sfn|Myers|2013}} Structurally, it is largely composed of the chords of D and E♭ that are performed by Cavaliere on his piano during the choruses in a {{music|time|6|8}} time signature before alternating.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} During the verses, the chord of F♯ largely substitutes the chord of D, though also marks the appearance of the chords of G and A through a modulation that appears towards the end of the verses.{{Sfn|Cornish|Miller|2019|p=153}} "Groovin{{'"}} bears a strong inspiration from Afro-Cuban music,{{Sfn|Rhino|2021}} particularly concerning its baião rhythm and instrumentation which was unconventional for the band.{{Sfn|Myers|2016|p=88}} It features the use of conga drums played by drummer Dino Danelli and tambourine by Cornish rather than a more standard drum set.{{Sfn|Myers|2016|p=88}}

sections.heading: Recording
Release and commercial performance
Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
Upon initial release in 1967, "Groovin{{'"}} received critical acclaim by critics, many of whom noted the apparent change in genres for the Young Rascals. The review panel in ''Billboard'' magazine noted it, considering it to be an "easy-go ballad" and "smooth summertime blockbuster" that was both aptly titled and better than their previous single.<ref name=":5">{{Cite magazine |date=April 15, 1967 |title=Pop Spotlights |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1967/Billboard%201967-04-15.pdf |magazine=Billboard |page=18 |via=WorldRadioHistory}}</ref> ''Billboard'' additionally predicted it to become a top-20 hit in the US.<ref name=":5" /> ''Cash Box'' magazine held a similar sentiment, the reviewer also noting the change in genres, with them stating it to be an "easy-going, smooth, rhythmic" ballad.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |date=April 15, 1967 |title=Pick of The Week |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/60s/1967/CB-1967-04-15.pdf |journal=Cash Box |page=24 |via=WorldRadioHistory}}</ref> ''Cash Box'' accurately predicted it to become a chart topper.<ref name=":6" /> The review panel for ''[[Record World]]'' magazine stated that "Groovin{{'"}} was a perfect record for teenagers to "do their dancing to".<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |date=April 15, 1967 |title=Four Star Pick |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/60s/67/RW-1967-04-15.pdf |journal=[[Record World]] |page=6 |via=WorldRadioHistory}}</ref> They awarded it a four-star rating.<ref name=":7" />

Among British critics, Dave Munde of British group [[the Tremeloes]] found "Groovin{{'"}} to be a great song by a "tremendously underrated group" while reviewing for [[NME|''New Musical Express'']].<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Munden |first=Dave |date=June 3, 1967 |title=Top Ten of the top group The Tremeloes |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/New-Musical-Express/1967/NME-1967-06-03-S-OCR.pdf |journal=[[NME|New Musical Express]] |page=3 |via=WorldRadioHistory}}</ref> Munden found the track great enough that he hoped the Tremeloes could record a cover of it.<ref name=":8" /> In a blind review for ''[[Melody Maker]]'', disc jockey [[Pete Murray (DJ)|Pete Murray]] found "Groovin{{'"}} to be "the best record the Young Rascals have ever done", stating that it was "a great number" and that he otherwise didn't like the group's music.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Murray |first=Peter |author-link=Pete Murray (DJ) |date=May 20, 1967 |title=Blind Date |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Melody-Maker/60s/67/Melody-Maker-1967-0520.pdf |journal=[[Melody Maker]] |page=10 |via=WorldRadioHistory}}</ref> Some British critics additionally commented on the lyrical and musical tone of the song, including Richard Williams of ''[[The Guardian]]'', who wrote that Cavaliere's "husky voice" gave "the tune a very sunny feeling", writing that the song was "beautiful".<ref>{{cite news |author1=Williams |first=Richard |date=June 3, 1967 |title=New Releases |page=4 |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-guardian-journal-the-young-rascals/130416920/ |access-date=August 21, 2023 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The lyrics were positively reviewed by the Upon initial release in 1967, "Groovin{{'"}} received critical acclaim by critics, many of whom noted the apparent change in genres for the Young Rascals. The review panel in Billboard magazine noted it, considering it to be an "easy-go ballad" and "smooth summertime blockbuster" that was both aptly titled and better than their previous single. Billboard additionally predicted it to become a top-20 hit in the US. Cash Box magazine held a similar sentiment, the reviewer also noting the change in genres, with them stating it to be an "easy-going, smooth, rhythmic" ballad. Cash Box accurately predicted it to become a chart topper. The review panel for Record World magazine stated that "Groovin{{'"}} was a perfect record for teenagers to "do their dancing to". They awarded it a four-star rating.

Among British critics, Dave Munde of British group the Tremeloes found "Groovin{{'"}} to be a great song by a "tremendously underrated group" while reviewing for New Musical Express. Munden found the track great enough that he hoped the Tremeloes could record a cover of it. In a blind review for Melody Maker, disc jockey Pete Murray found "Groovin{{'"}} to be "the best record the Young Rascals have ever done", stating that it was "a great number" and that he otherwise didn't like the group's music. Some British critics additionally commented on the lyrical and musical tone of the song, including Richard Williams of The Guardian, who wrote that Cavaliere's "husky voice" gave "the tune a very sunny feeling", writing that the song was "beautiful". The lyrics were positively reviewed by the Whitstable Times, who called the song "slow" but predicted it to become the Young Rascals' first British hit.

On April 26, 1967, [[Booker T. & the M.G.'s]] recorded an instrumental version of "Groovin{{'"}} at the [[Stax Museum of American Soul Music|Stax Recording Studios]] in [[Memphis, Tennessee]], together with what would make up the majority of the group's fifth studio album ''[[Hip Hug-Her]]'' (1967).{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|loc=insert 2}} The recording was produced by [[Stax Records]]'s co-founder [[Jim Stewart (record producer)|Jim Stewart]] in what was his final recording session with the band.{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|p=1}}

The group's rendition of "Groovin{{'"}} is re-arranged to fit their more [[instrumental rock]] and soul-inspired sound, featuring a conventional [[drum kit]] played by [[Al Jackson Jr.]], while [[Donald "Duck" Dunn]] provides bass and [[Booker T. Jones]] mirrors the original's vocal line on the [[Hammond organ|Hammond B-3 organ]].{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|p=2}} On the recording, the band's guitarist [[Steve Cropper]] over-dubbed piano as well as his regular guitar.{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|loc=insert 2}} According to Unterberger, Booker T's rendition of the song was a tribute for the Young Rascals, who idolized the band and other rhythm and blues bands.{{Sfn|Unterberger|2007b|p=1}} "Groovin{{'"}} was initially released on May 23, 1967 as part of the ''Hip Hug-Her'' album, where it appeared as track three on the album's second side.{{Sfn|Unterberger|2007b|p=1}}{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|loc=back cover}}

On June 12, 1967, while the Young Rascals original performance of "Groovin{{'"}} was at number two on the ''Billboard'' chart,{{Sfn|Whitburn|1990|pp=523–524}} Stax released Booker T. & the M.G.'s rendition of the song as a single, backed by "Slim Jenkin's Place", an original [[instrumental]] composed by the four members of the band.{{Sfn|Rhino|1992|loc=insert 2}} It debuted on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 on August 5, 1967 at a position of 86, before reaching its peak of number 21 on September 23, 1967.{{Sfn|Whitburn|1990|p=211}} It dropped off the charts on October 21, 1967, having spent 12 weeks on the charts.{{Sfn|Whitburn|1990|p=211}} Elsewhere, it also peaked at number ten on the ''Billboard'' [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|Hot Rhythm & Blues Singles]] charts,{{Sfn|Whitburn|2017|p=135}} and also reached number two on the Canadian ''RPM'' chart.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=October 14, 1967 |title=The RPM 100 |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/CANADA/RPM/60s/1967/RPM-1967-10-14.pdf |journal=RPM |page=5 |via=WorldMediaHistory}}</ref> The B-side was the side that charted in the UK, reaching number 58 on the ''Record Retailer'' chart, and also reached number 70 on the Hot Rhythm & Blues Singles in the US.{{Sfn|Whitburn|2017|p=135}}{{Sfn|Brown|2000|p=187}}
